The Chainlink DON-operated `KeystoneForwarder` delivers that report here via `onReport`. Extends `ReceiverTemplate` (`src/cre/ReceiverTemplate.sol`) \u2014 vendored verbatim from the official `keeper-bot-ts` CRE template generated by `cre init` against a real, authenticated Chainlink account, not reconstructed from a paraphrase of the docs \u2014 rather than reimplementing `IReceiver` from scratch. That gets this contract the sponsor's own forwarder-address validation (updatable post-deployment via `Ownable`, in case Chainlink ever rotates the Forwarder) and optional workflow-author/name/id pinning for free, instead of a bespoke, unaudited-by-anyone-but-us version of the same check. On top of that template, this contract is deliberately a **closed dispatcher, not a generic relayer**: `_processReport` cannot be made to carry arbitrary `(target, calldata)` \u2014 only one of six named `Action`s against one of two fixed, immutable contract addresses set at deployment. This is a narrower, safer surface than \"forward whatever calldata the report contains,\" and it costs nothing here because the six targets are a closed, known set: every function this contract can ever call is already callable by literally anyone today (that is the entire point of them being permissionless). Spoofing a call to this receiver directly (bypassing the Forwarder \u2014 blocked by `ReceiverTemplate`'s own check, but suppose it weren't) grants an attacker nothing beyond what they could already do by calling `claimDefault` etc. themselves \u2014 there is no privilege escalation here, only convenience and
